https://www.telegraph.co.uk/snooker/2023.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters stopped play at the World Snooker Championship on Monday after storming the Crucible theatre in Sheffield and pouring orange powder over one of the tables.
The match between Joe Perry and Robert Milkins had to be suspended after a man stood on the table and emptied a bag of the bright orange substance before being dragged away by security officials.
A woman also began climbing onto another snooker table, where Mark Allen was playing Fan Zhengyi, but was bundled away by tournament staff.
Officials, including master of ceremonies and BBC commentator Rob Walker, then emerged with vacuum cleaners and rubber gloves in an attempt to clear up the powder and get play restarted.
The green baize cloth will be reclothed ahead of Tuesday's matches.
The two protesters, who were wearing ‘Just Stop Oil’ T-shirts, were detained backstage by stewards and later arrested. Boos and shouts of “get him off” could be heard from inside the arena in response to the protesters’ actions.
The official ‘Just Stop Oil’ Twitter account later posted a message saying that “new oil and gas will snooker us”.
Stephen Hendry, the seven times world snooker champion, called the interruption “scary”.
“It's a first. It is scary. Wow,” he said. “It caught us all by surprise.”
Campaign group Just Stop Oil said the stunt was intended to draw attention to its demands that the Government immediately stop all new UK fossil fuel projects.
It also urged UK sporting institutions to “step into civil resistance against the Government's genocidal policies”.
World Snooker Tour officials confirmed that the match between Allen and Zhengyi was set to resume after a delay of approximately 45 minutes.
This attack on the table will raise major questions over tournament security.
The World Snooker Championships have previously been disturbed by a streaker before the 2008 final between Ronnie O’Sullivan and Ali Carter and even a pigeon, but have never been targeted in this way by environmental or political campaigners.
The first session of the first-round match between Perry and Milkins, which had only just started, was abandoned after the interruption.
It will be replayed on Tuesday evening and the second session will start on Thursday at 9.30am after a highly unusual full day between sessions.
Fan and Allen returned on Monday to a standing ovation. Allen, who had been on a break of 24, was unaffected by the drama and promptly made a frame-winning clearance to pink of 126.
Speaking after he returned to claim a 10-5 victory over Fan, Allen said: "I think I was the last person in the whole arena to work out what was going on because I was focused on the shot I was about to play.
"I heard a bang, that I thought it was on the other table and then I turned round and there was a woman on my table.
"It could have been a lot worse - you saw what happened on the other table and how much disruption it caused.
"It was a surreal moment but I feel like even talking about it is giving them airtime they don't deserve because they are just idiots. What are they trying to gain from what they have done? I am sure there are better ways to get their point across."
World Snooker later tweeted: "This is the Crucible. The show will go on."
South Yorkshire Police said a 30-year-old man and a 52-year-old woman were arrested on Monday on suspicion of criminal damage.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/snooker/2023.title: John Virgo and Dennis Taylor on their BBC stay of execution – ‘Age should not come into it’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/snooker/2023.subtitle: The pair have reached near-legendary status in the BBC commentary box and have got no intention of going anywhere soon
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/snooker/2023.text:
You can safely claim to have achieved popular “cut-through” when the longest-serving prime minister for 200 years specifically asks to sit with you and then clasps your hand throughout a firework display.
Or when 18.5 million people stay up after midnight to watch you play a snooker match and, some 38 years later, can still tell you exactly where they were at the moment it happened.
John Virgo and Dennis Taylor are exchanging stories inside Sheffield’s Crucible Theatre about how snooker went from a largely unseen pastime in working men’s clubs to its status for a period during the 1980s as the nation’s leading sporting obsession.
“Jim Davidson was a big Tory supporter – this Crafty Cockney Conservative,” Virgo says, recalling how he came to spend a surreal evening with Davidson, his co-host on the primetime Big Break quiz show, and Margaret Thatcher.
“Mrs Thatcher was, ‘Oh, we love that television show you do, Jim’. She then turned to her husband Denis and was, ‘Who’s that snooker player we like Denis? John Virgo. We love him’. She held my hand for five minutes while we watched the fireworks.
“I’m this dour northern socialist and all I’m thinking is, ‘I hope my pals in Salford don’t see me holding Mrs Thatcher’s hand’.”
Taylor giggles, before recalling how he accepted offers onto every conceivable television show after beating Steve Davis on that unforgettable black-ball finish in 1985. “I went on Wogan three times in a year and did trick-shots with Sooty and Sweep,” he says.
When the Hollywood star Paul Newman was in England to promote The Color of Money film, he told BBC presenter Barry Norman that he had been jumping up and down on his hotel bed in excitement at watching the conclusion of Taylor’s 1987 Masters victory against Alex Higgins.
Virgo and Taylor have been returning to the same spiritual home now for 46 of their 50-year friendship and were also among 16 hopefuls when the World Snooker Championship first moved to Sheffield in 1977. “Remember the creaky floor?” Virgo says. “If you had Bill Werbeniuk on one side, and Len Ganley refereeing, it was like a herd of wildebeest. A lot of people questioned the wisdom when we first came here. All a bit strange… but it worked. Thank goodness.”
They have both also been behind the microphone now for enough decades to stand comparison with the great doyens of sports commentary – men such as John Arlott or Dan Maskell – and the welcome news is that forecasts of their demise have proved premature.
Virgo and Taylor had expected 2022 to be their last. Then this year was supposed to be their swansong but, after almost two years thinking that the end was nigh, news has arrived of an indefinite stay of execution.
“It’s carrying on as normal for the foreseeable future: That was the message, thankfully,” Virgo says. “It was music to our ears. We love the game.” Taylor nods and is still sure that nobody can read snooker better than them.
“Age shouldn't have anything to do with it,” he says. They had not planned to go public in 2021 with whispers that they would be leaving. Virgo had simply answered a straight question with what was a straight and gracious answer – “I understand, nothing lasts forever” – but it did then prompt a huge backlash against the idea that they would be yet more BBC veterans moved on.
“All of a sudden there was a bit of an outcry on Twitter,” Virgo says. “We discussed it. ‘Do you think it was the right thing to say [publicly]?’ but as it turned out it was the right thing. It put it out there. People give their opinion. Otherwise we could have just drifted away. ‘Hang on, where are they this year?’”
Their combined years are now in advance of a maximum 147 break but an hour in their company provides a captivating reminder of what would have been squandered. Humour, knowledge, experience, natural story-telling and, above all, an insight into snooker and wider British culture that provides an unbroken personal link from Joe and Fred Davis all the way to Ronnie O’Sullivan and Judd Trump.
The response in the live shows that they still perform with Steve Davis to standing ovations all over the country has further demonstrated what snooker fans think. “When we say we are still going to be here [on television], they cheer,” Taylor says.
Further shows are planned after this year’s World Championship (which include old haunts such as Reading’s Hexagon Theatre and the Crucible itself) and it is these exhibitions that actually still tell you most about what made their generation so golden.
They were fierce competitors, for sure, but they were also entertainers in an era when sport was operating without the sense of entitlement that so often now pervades. When Taylor reached the final of Pot Black in 1975, he wrote to hundreds of snooker clubs in an effort to get work.
He funded his entry into the World Championship in Australia that year by personally organising 10 shows at a Lancashire brewery. As part of his sales pitch, Virgo would challenge a club’s best players at exhibitions to a combined 200 start and offer to give back his appearance money if he lost. He also started perfecting impersonations of his fellow professionals that would eventually be showcased on the BBC.
They both worked in holiday camps, where Taylor discovered that telling Irish jokes whenever he missed a trick shot would engage the crowd. “If I’d got a new gag, you’d try it at 10am,” he says. “If it worked at that time, you could keep it in. Tell a story, entertain people, make them smile.”
“We were trying to sell the game, make it watchable, and we were lucky to have this contrast of characters,” adds Virgo, who describes the infamous Alex Higgins as the “icing on the cake” for a sport yearning for popular exposure.
They both then puff out their cheeks before recounting a random series of Alex Higgins stories. There was the ‘A HIGGINS’ ink stamp that he had specially made in Hong Kong and briefly insisted upon using instead of hand-signing the mass of autograph requests.
Then there was the day he won a week’s supply of pie and beer in the snooker club he frequented with Taylor after answering the owner’s challenge for eight century breaks in an afternoon. “He had this panache that I’ve never seen in anybody else and he was as bright as a button,” Virgo says.
“He could do The Times crossword. He brought people on board to love the game and yet, if everyone was like him, the game would finish in ruins.
“I always prefix it in the show now by asking Dennis, ‘What was your history with Alex?’ And he replies, ‘What, apart from him threatening to have me shot?’” Taylor smiles and then adds: “And Steve Davis always says, ‘We don’t have any characters any more. We don’t have anybody who goes up and headbutts the tournament director or punches the referees’.”
Handling Higgins, Virgo says, proved to be the perfect training for his second career on Big Break and then in pantomime with Davidson. “I had one advantage with Jim. I’d worked with Higgins. Because he [Davidson] could turn on a sixpence when he went out in company. Just like Higgins. But he couldn’t be worse than him. So it wasn’t going to affect me.”
And what is Virgo’s strategy for dealing with a temperamental social partner? “Just blank them and walk away,” he says. “A lot of people run after them.”
Both Taylor and Virgo started commentating while they were still players in the 1980s and have never received any instructions from the BBC hierarchy.
“Snooker was one of the first where we introduced a bit of humour into the commentary,” Taylor says. “I’ve always gone in and chatted as if it was watching with someone in their living room.”
Virgo remembers being advised by the legendary ‘whispering’ Ted Lowe to “let the pictures do the talking”, but recalls how that style once fell foul of a North American director.
“We were in Thailand and Ted and I hadn’t said a word for 30 seconds. All of a sudden this director was shouting in our ear, ‘Have the commentators died in there?’”
Virgo is also all about providing soothing colour, context and emotion rather than machine-gunning statistics into the viewers’ ears. “Be welcoming. Make it watchable. Get the viewer involved. I find a lot of the time it’s people telling you about stats from 15, 20 years ago and it’s like it’s getting in the way of what is happening on the table.”
Taylor believes that the art of commentary is to step in when the viewer is unsure what will happen next. It has been a typically eventful fortnight, with everything from a maximum 147 break, the shock of Ronnie O’Sullivan’s sudden exit and a Just Stop Oil protester throwing orange paint powder across a table.
And yet, as they nod and say hello to just about every person who walks through the Crucible foyer while we talk, the overwhelming impression is of two grandees at the head of a constantly evolving family.
“We’ve known these lads since they were kids - going through all the emotion when they were winning, and hardly ever spoke to anybody,” Virgo says, ahead of catching up later that evening with Davis, Stephen Hendry, John Parrott and Ken Doherty.
“The game has given us everything. It’s been a remarkable journey… and we are still going. How long that lasts, I don’t know. But, as Dennis always says, we’ll keep talking until they tell us to stop.”

The London Marathon is under threat from protesters after Just Stop Oil raised fears of a chaotic summer of sport.
After halting play at the World Snooker Championships on Monday by throwing orange-coloured powder over a table, environmental activists have promised ongoing disruption to major sporting events unless the Government changes its oil and gas policy.
Marathon organisers are working with the police to prevent disruption and have received assurances that a separate environmental protest planned by Extinction Rebellion, which is expected to attract 30,000 people, will not target Sunday’s event.
However, after storming the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield on Monday, the Just Stop Oil group has raised fears for both the London Marathon and FA Cup this weekend, as well as major forthcoming events like Wimbledon, the British Open golf and Formula One’s British Grand Prix.
“There will be ongoing disruption until the Government meets our demand to end new oil and gas,” the activist group said when asked about further disruption at sporting events.
With FA Cup semi-finals also being played on Saturday and Sunday in front of almost 90,000 people at Wembley Stadium, the Metropolitan Police have major security operations in place this weekend. The marathon starts on Sunday morning but the 50,000 field – as well as friends, family and supporters – will be descending on the capital throughout the days building up the race.
Extinction Rebellion has been planning “The Big One” – a four-day period of action from Friday until Monday – for several weeks.
Extinction Rebellion conceded that the event could cause “logistical disruption” but said that it will “coexist” with the London Marathon, which raises millions of pounds each year for charity.
Greenpeace, Friends of the Earth and PCS Union have been named among groups planning to join the gathering throughout Westminster and at the Houses of Parliament. Just Stop Oil are not listed as participants on the Extinction Rebellion’s website.
When pressed on specific plans for Sunday, when four-times Olympic champion Mo Farah will be among the London Marathon field, Just Stop Oil added: “We will continue to disrupt sports and cultural events until the institutions join us in civil resistance against our genocidal government’s plans to licence new oil and gas. We expect that there will be lots of Just Stop Oil supporters at the London Marathon. If the polls are right then about 60 per cent of the London Marathon runners support our demand to stop new oil and gas.”
Hugh Brasher, event director for the London Marathon, has been in discussions with Extinction Rebellion and warned spectators to avoid the Parliament Square area.
“The Extinction Rebellion organisers have assured us that they do not wish to disrupt the TCS London Marathon,” he said. “As Parliament Square and the immediate surrounding area will be very busy, we advise spectators to watch the London Marathon from other locations. As always, we are working closely with the Metropolitan Police and other stakeholders on the safety and security of the event.”
Extinction Rebellion activists, meanwhile, vowed to “step up campaigns in new and inventive ways” unless the Government stops the search for new fossil fuels and creates “emergency citizens’ assemblies to let the people decide how to end the fossil fuel era quickly and fairly”.
The activists said the four days of protest, from Friday to Monday, “are not intended for public disruption” but have promised a plan for “the greatest acts of civil disobedience in this country’s history” within three months if their demands are not met by Monday at 5pm.
“We will be taking more radical action because the clock is ticking for every human and non-human alive today,” said organisers of the Extinction Rebellion protest. “We are not going to stand quietly by while time runs out and we all face the worst suffering possible.”
Fears around fresh sabotage attempts come after the Grand National was disrupted by animal rights activists just two days before the Just Stop Oil campaigner covered a snooker table with orange power paint.
A woman also began climbing onto a second snooker table but was bundled away by tournament staff.
A 25-year-old man and 52-year-old woman were arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage after gaining entry to the Crucible Theatre and have both been bailed by Yorkshire police
World Snooker introduced beefed up security measures following Monday’s chaos, and have outlawed large bags in the arena and introduced extra security staff and more extensive searches.
When asked whether disruption at Aintree had been a factor in the group causing chaos at the Crucible, a Just Stop Oil spokeswoman said: “We will not answer questions about how we plan our actions. That is irrelevant when we face crop failure, drought and starvation within a few short decades. To allow new oil and gas is the greatest criminal act in human history. It's time for everyone to join us in civil resistance or face the loss of everything we know and love. Which side are you on?”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/politics/202.text:
Rishi Sunak was escorted through central London by a “North Korean-style” motorcade featuring dozens of jogging police officers in a bid to evade Extinction Rebellion.
A fleet of cars containing the Prime Minister was spotted on Sunday - the day of the London marathon - surrounded by one set of policemen on bicycles and another on foot.
A video shared on Twitter showed one police officer on a bike leading the convoy, shouting “out of the way please”.
The policemen were followed by a series of cars and then officers on motorbikes. A police car brings up the rear, with more police officers running at pace behind.
A government source said it was believed the Metropolitan Police’s tactics were to help the convoy evade protestors from Extinction Rebellion, who had threatened to disrupt the marathon.
It was not thought that the tactics were a new standard, the source said.
It is possible that having officers on foot and bikes may have allowed them to intervene more quickly to any protest, and possibly with less risk, than if they were in patrol cars or on motorbikes.
Asked whether the bizarre escort was related to Extinction Rebellion, the Prime Minister’s official spokesman said: “On security issues, that is one for the Met Police, rather than us.”
The Metropolitan Police however declined to comment on “matters of private security”.
Social media users were baffled by the large escort, describing it as “a tremendous waste of police manpower”.
Others compared it to the moment 12 bodyguards dressed in suits ran in formation alongside North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un’s car as he left a meeting with his South Korean counterpart in 2018.
One Twitter user wrote: “Not necessary at all. I can’t understand how this is a good use of the few police officers we have.”
Another said: “This escort looks like something out of North Korea but with less fit and fewer good looking bodyguards.”
Another added: “The difference between North Korea and Rishi Sunak's regime? About 20 BMI.” A third said: “Looks like a homage to Pyongyang on military parade day.”

Farah was caught and passed by two other British athletes - Emile Cairess after 15 miles and then Phil Sesemann on the final sprint up The Mall - before finishing ninth. He wobbled like an exhausted prize-fighter as he crossed the line but, amid a rapturous reception through the streets of London, it had been an admirable swansong. Now 40, Farah said that it was the people - and even the memory of the London 2012 Olympics, where he won double gold over 5,000m and 10,000m - that sustained him.
"Part of me wanted to cry along the course,” said Farah. “I’ll never forget that crowd. I wanted to drop out. But so many people came out to support me. I just wanted to say thank-you. This city is incredible. There is no place like home. Whenever I can’t motivate myself, have struggles, I think back to that crowd.
“It is emotional. I started here in the mini marathon... I would never have believed I could be Olympic champion. I never thought I could challenge the Kenyans and the Ethiopians, until I started living and training with them and training. I don’t have regrets - as an athlete you have to make mistakes to be the best.”
The race was won by Kelvin Kiptum, Kenya’s 23-year-old marathon sensation, in an extraordinary course record time of 2hr 1min 25sec that was only 16 seconds outside Eliud Kipchoge's world record. Kiptum was already the fastest marathon debutant in history and, having made a relatively cautious start, broke clear after 30km to run the second half of the race in less than an hour. It was almost two minutes faster than he had run the opening 13.1 miles on what was supposedly the slower half of the course.
It was also a performance which suggests that he has the talent to not just surpass Kipchoge as the fastest marathon runner of all-time, but become the first runner under two hours in any conventional competitive race. Kipchoge, who is a four-time winner of the London Marathon and the double reigning Olympic champion, famously became the first runner under two hours in a special paced event in Vienna in 2019.
Kiptum said that he had been unaware of the time and how close he was to the world record as he put almost three minutes into compatriot Geoffrey Kamworor during an incredible 12 kilometre surge to the finish.

If all goes to plan on Sunday, Chris Thompson will run another marathon in London that puts him in contention for a third Olympics before spending even longer cheering home his mum in the same race.
Thompson was Great Britain’s sole marathon finisher in Tokyo and, proving that Olympians can inspire previous as well as future generations, his mum Wendy suddenly surprised him.
“We were chatting one day and she said, 'I'd love to run a marathon',” he says. “It was two or three years ago. Even parkrun she had never done because she was too intimidated to run with people. She wanted to put her headphones on and not be seen. My dad got her treadmill. Now she has done 3½ hour runs. She kept putting off the thought of doing it. She finally got in. And so it was on Thursday that Wendy, who is 65, joined Chris on the train to London from Thatcham to the London Marathon Expo to collect their race numbers. "Before we ran in Rio at the Olympic 10,000, now he comes to the marathon," Tola explained.
"He is more experienced in 10,000. Maybe on Sunday he will run together with us and we will stay together. I hope (this) for him."
Meanwhile, Kelvin Kiptum, who ran the third-fastest ever marathon time in Valencia in December, is excited to compete against Farah for the first time.
Kiptum added: "Of course I saw Mo Farah, still I was young. He was a great athlete. One time I used to say I will compete with Mo Farah so I am very excited to race with him."
The man himself said: "It will be my last marathon. After that I will do a couple more races, it hasn't been announced yet and I will not announce it yet but in terms of marathons, this is it.
"I do owe it for the British crowd and the people who supported me throughout my journey. From a young boy to someone who became four-time Olympic champion and that Super Saturday, the crowd and the people in the stadium did follow my journey.
"For me it is a great way to end my marathon career here. This is where it started with the mini-marathon that took place and I won. Then going onto the seniors and finishing third in 2018, that was my best but age catches up with us all.
"The key thing is to make the most of it, enjoy it and I am sure the crowd will make a big difference for me on Sunday. As you get to the last 10km, the last six miles, I know it will be tough.
"I would love to give back to the community, to young kids and become a coach or development coach. I want to continue to give back the skills and tools I have learnt.
"What motivates me is seeing young athletes coming along and having that energy. If I can give something to those young athletes and take them to the next level, I would love to do that."
